# Working with an agent
Practical advice for this afternoon

## Three ways in

::: {.compact .wide}
| | Web chat ([claude.ai]{.muted}) | Desktop app: *Chat* or *Cowork* mode | Claude Code ([terminal, IDE, or Desktop app *Code* mode]{.muted}) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sees your files** | What you upload | Folders you connect (Cowork) | Your project directory |
| **Runs code** | In a sandbox, not your environment | In a sandboxed VM (Cowork) | In *your* environment, with your pixi env |
| **Results** | Download them | Written to the folder | Edits in the repo, git commits |
| **Your tools** ([git, pytest, CLAUDE.md, CI]{.muted}) | No | Partly | Yes |
:::

::: {.panel .compact .wide}
The Desktop app has three modes: *Chat* · *Cowork* · **Code**.
Only **Code** is Claude Code. Chat and Cowork belong in the middle column.
:::

::: notes
Everything in the cases (oracle tests, validation documents, the git log) needs the right-hand column.
Cowork is the Desktop app's agentic mode for knowledge work. Its shell runs in a
VM with restricted network: git push and package publishing are blocked, and it doesn't
read the Claude Code settings in ~/.claude. It's fine for documents; for code, use Code mode.
The web chat can run Python in a sandbox, but on uploaded copies of your files, not in your environment.
:::

## Why not the web chat?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.panel .compact}
**Agent in your environment**

1. Edits the code
2. Runs `pytest`, reads the failure
3. Fixes, runs again
4. Commits when green

[The agent closes the loop. You review the result.]{.accent-strong}
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.panel .compact}
**Web chat**

1. Writes the code
2. *You* copy it out and run it
3. *You* paste the error back
4. Repeat

[You are the loop. In practice: one shot or nothing.]{.accent-strong}
:::
:::
::::

::: {.wide}
[None of the scaffolding (pixi, pytest, ruff, Quarto, CI) helps if the agent can't run it.
Fine for questions and small snippets; not for building software.]{.muted}
:::

::: notes
There is no git history, no CLAUDE.md, no tests the agent can run, and every round trip
goes through you. The jaxdft git log (73 commits in 9 days) is only possible because the
agent ran the tests itself after every change.
The same applies to the Desktop app's Chat mode.
:::

## Terminal or Desktop app?

::: {.panel .compact .wide}
In the Desktop app, switch to **Code** mode. The default *Chat* mode is the web chat in a window.
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.panel .compact}
**Desktop app, Code mode**

- Visual diff review, with comments on lines
- Parallel sessions in a sidebar, each in its own git worktree if you want
- Preview pane for web pages
- No terminal needed
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.panel .compact}
**Terminal (`claude`)**

- Runs wherever you have a shell
- Scriptable: `claude -p "..."`
- Runs in CI (GitHub Actions)
- Same in VS Code / JetBrains
:::
:::
::::

::: {.wide}
[Both are **Claude Code** working on the same project. Pick whichever you prefer.]{.muted}
:::

::: notes
Desktop can also start cloud sessions that keep running after you close the app.
Sources: code.claude.com/docs/en/desktop, code.claude.com/docs/en/headless (checked 2026-11-24).
:::

## Permissions: what it may do without asking

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%" .compact}
[It runs in *your* environment, so it asks first]{.accent-strong}

**No prompt:** reading project files; read-only commands (`ls`, `grep`, `git status`).

**Asks:** editing files, other commands, web pages.

- *Yes*: this once
- *Yes, and don't ask again for* `pixi run *`: saved for this repo
- *No*: press **Tab** first to tell it what to do instead
- **Esc** declines too

**Shift+Tab** switches mode (shown under the prompt box).
:::

::: {.column width="52%" .compact}
| Mode | Asks before |
|---|---|
| **Manual** | Edits and commands |
| **Accept edits** | Commands only |
| **Plan** | Nothing: it can't edit yet |
| **Auto** | Nothing: a classifier checks each action, [no guarantee]{.muted} |

[`.claude/settings.json`, committed and shared:]{.muted}

```json
{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": ["Bash(pixi run *)"],
    "deny": ["Bash(git push --force *)",
             "Read(./.env)"]
  }
}
```

[Rules are enforced, unlike `CLAUDE.md`. Deny beats allow.]{.muted}
:::
::::

::: notes
--dangerously-skip-permissions turns all of this off: only ever inside a container or VM.
Recent versions start new sessions in auto mode, so people may never see a prompt.
For a first session I'd switch to Manual (Shift+Tab) to watch what it actually does,
then allow-list the routine commands (pixi run *). To make Manual the default for a project:
"defaultMode": "default" under permissions in .claude/settings.json.
"Don't ask again" for a command is saved to .claude/settings.local.json (personal, not committed);
file-edit approvals only last for the session.
/permissions shows and edits all the rules. Order: deny, then ask, then allow.
The template already denies force-push and git reset --hard.
/sandbox restricts shell commands to the project directory and an allow-listed network.
Source: code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes, /permissions, /settings, /sandboxing (checked 2026-11-25).
:::

## What goes in `CLAUDE.md`

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%" .compact}
[Read at the start of every session]{.accent-strong}

Put in what should shape the agent's decisions in *every* session.

**Done means:** the exact commands that must pass.

**Conventions** no linter checks: units, array shapes, commits.

**Context:** a few lines, and pointers to the spec. Not the roadmap.

**Integrity:** never tune a constant to pass a test (Nguyen's α).

**When to stop and ask.**

**Leave out:** what the code already shows, and anything that changes weekly.

[Grow it from failures. It is advice, not enforcement: run the checks in hooks and CI too.]{.muted}
:::

::: {.column width="58%"}
```markdown
# CLAUDE.md

## Project
relaxkit: geometry optimisation for molecules, in JAX.
Spec and validation documents live in docs/ (Quarto).
Correctness first, then speed.

## Done means
- `pixi run test`, `pixi run lint` and `pixi run typecheck` pass
- New behaviour has a test; new physics has a validation document

## Conventions
- Atomic units internally; convert only at input and output
- Positions have shape (n_atoms, 3)
- One commit per logical change; the message says why

## Never
- Tune a constant or tolerance to make a test pass.
  Stop and report the discrepancy.
- Skip or weaken a failing test

## Stop and ask
- After three failed attempts at the same fix
- If the spec looks wrong, or before changing a public API
```
:::
::::

::: notes
The test for each line: does it change what the agent does in a typical session?
"Correctness first, then speed" does; a roadmap doesn't, and goes stale. Link to it instead.
Formatting rules ruff enforces don't need to be here.
The best lines are added after the agent gets something wrong twice; rules written in
advance tend to be generic. Keep it short: the longer it gets, the less weight each line carries.
The "Never" and "Stop and ask" sections are Nguyen's fudge factor and 33 stuck sessions, written as rules.
:::

## Plan mode: agree before it edits

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%" .compact}
[Try this today]{.accent-strong}

In plan mode the agent reads the code, explores, and writes a **plan**,
but **does not edit** your files until you approve.

**Alignment:** you see *its* understanding of the task before any code exists.
Misreadings of the physics are cheap to fix in a plan, expensive in a diff.

**Reviewability:** you review the approach first, so the diff that follows
is the one you expected.

**Not happy?** Choose *keep planning* and say what's wrong.
Iterate on the plan, not the code.

[In my experience: far better results on anything non-trivial.]{.muted}
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.panel .compact}
**Getting in**

- Terminal: **Shift+Tab** cycles modes until `⏸ plan mode on`
- Or one prompt: `/plan add smearing to the SCF loop`
- Desktop (Code mode): mode selector under the prompt box (**Cmd+Shift+M**)
- VS Code: mode indicator at the bottom of the prompt box
:::

::: {.panel .compact}
**When the plan is ready**

- *Yes, auto-accept edits*: go
- *Yes, manually approve edits*: review each one
- *No, keep planning*: give feedback
- **Ctrl+G**: edit the plan yourself first
:::
:::
::::

::: notes
This is step 1 of my loop ("Spec") made concrete: the plan is where I check that the agent
put the domain knowledge where it belongs, before any tests or code exist.
Rule of thumb: use it whenever the task is more than a one-line fix, or whenever you
couldn't describe the diff you expect in a sentence.
Approval option names vary a little with version and settings (e.g. "Yes, and use auto mode"
when auto mode is available). Desktop calls the default mode "Manual".
Start every session in plan mode: claude --permission-mode plan.
Source: code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes, /desktop, /vs-code (checked 2026-11-25).
:::

## Plan mode asks before it guesses

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%" .compact}
[`/plan add smearing to the SCF loop`]{.muted}

While planning, the agent stops to ask about the choices that are **yours to make**:
typically 3–4 options, each with its trade-off, and one marked *Recommended*.

**Domain knowledge goes in here,** at the point where the agent would otherwise pick silently.

**A wrong recommendation is a signal:** the agent is missing context.
Answer, then add it to `CLAUDE.md` or the spec.

**None fit?** Type your own answer.
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}
```text
 ←  ☐ Scheme  ☐ Width  ✔ Submit  →

Which smearing scheme should set the occupations?

❯ 1. Fermi-Dirac (Recommended)
     Width is a physical electronic temperature;
     the free energy has a clear meaning.
  2. Gaussian
     Simple and widely used; the width is not a
     temperature, so extrapolate to zero width.
  3. Marzari-Vanderbilt (cold)
     Small error in the energy for metals, and
     occupations stay between 0 and 1.
  4. Methfessel-Paxton
     Accurate for metals, but occupations can go
     negative; a poor fit for gapped systems.
  5. Type something.
```

[Illustrative: a made-up scenario, laid out like the terminal prompt.]{.muted .compact}
:::
::::

::: notes
The recommendation is a reasonable default for a molecular or general-purpose code, but
for metallic disordered systems you might well want cold smearing: exactly the kind of
choice that depends on what the code is for, which the agent can only guess.
The tabs at the top show it can batch several questions (here: scheme, then width and its units)
before it writes the plan.
If you never get questions, your prompt or spec may be doing the job already, or the
agent is making these choices silently: read the plan for them.
:::

## Drafting a spec: let it interview you

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%" .compact}
[When you don't know exactly what you want yet]{.accent-strong}

You don't have to work it all out before you prompt.
Ask the agent to **interview you**.

It asks multiple-choice questions about what you haven't pinned down,
and **keeps asking until the answers add up to a spec.**

Then **start a fresh session** to build from it:
a clean context, and a written definition of done.

The same file is what you check the result against.

[[Source: Claude Code best practices, *Brainstorm with Claude first*](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices#brainstorm-with-claude-first)]{.muted}
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
::: {.panel .compact}
**1 · Interview**

```text
I want to add the stress tensor to our DFT code
but haven't thought it through yet. Interview me
until you could write the spec, then write it to
docs/spec/stress.qmd.
```
:::

::: {.panel .compact}
**2 · Review the spec**

Short enough to read properly. Edit it: the decisions in it are yours.
:::

::: {.panel .compact}
**3 · Fresh session**

```text
/plan Implement docs/spec/stress.qmd
```
:::
:::
::::

::: notes
This is how I do the Spec step of my loop. The agent asks about the theory, the working
equations, units, which invariants and limits we can test; I answer. What comes out is a
spec short enough to review, with the domain decisions made by me, not guessed.
Writing it into the Quarto site means it is also the shared context from "My workflow".
The same prompt works for an implementation plan: "interview me until you could write the plan".
Source: code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices#brainstorm-with-claude-first (checked 2026-11-25).
:::

## Cheat sheet

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%" .compact}
**Steer**

| | |
|---|---|
| **Esc** | Stop it mid-task |
| **Esc Esc** | Rewind to an earlier point |
| `/rewind` | Same: code, conversation or both |
| **Shift+Tab** | Switch permission mode |
| `/plan` | Plan mode for one task |
| `/btw` | Side question, kept out of the context |
:::

::: {.column width="33%" .compact}
**Sessions & context**

| | |
|---|---|
| `/clear` | Fresh start, new task |
| `/compact` | Summarise to free context |
| `/context` | How full is the context? |
| `/resume` | Pick up an old session |
| `claude -c` | Continue the last one |
| `/diff` | What has it changed? |
:::

::: {.column width="33%" .compact}
**Input & setup**

| | |
|---|---|
| `@file` | Point it at a file |
| `!cmd` | Run a shell command yourself |
| **Ctrl+V** | Paste an image (a plot) |
| `/init` | Draft a `CLAUDE.md` |
| `/memory` | Edit `CLAUDE.md` |
| `/model`, `/usage` | Model; limits used |
| `/permissions` | Allow and deny rules |
| `/help` | Everything else |
:::
::::

::: {.wide}
[One task per session: `/clear` between tasks. Rewind only tracks Claude's own file edits, so commit often: git is the real undo.]{.muted}
:::

::: notes
Long sessions get worse as the context fills with old attempts; /clear is cheap.
/rewind does not undo changes made by shell commands, or edits you made yourself.
/doctor checks the installation if something seems broken.
Ctrl+G opens the prompt in your editor, useful for long prompts. Ctrl+R searches prompt history.
Source: code.claude.com/docs/en/commands, /interactive-mode, /checkpointing (checked 2026-11-25).
:::

## Getting started

::: {.panel .compact .wide}
**Template repository:** [github.com/tolborg-group/agentic-package-template](https://github.com/tolborg-group/agentic-package-template)

A starting `CLAUDE.md`, and pytest, ruff and mypy already configured with pixi.
:::

::: {.compact .wide}
1. Start from the template, and use **Claude Code** (terminal, IDE, or Desktop app **Code** mode)
2. Fill in `CLAUDE.md`: the project, what done means, your conventions
3. Pick a small first milestone, and decide where you check the agent's work
4. Start it in **plan mode**: agree on the plan before any code is written
5. Add to `CLAUDE.md` when the agent gets something wrong

[My loop is one way to do step 3, not the way. Try your own.]{.muted}
:::

::: notes
TODO: the template URL goes live once the repository is pushed.
"My workflow" is inspiration, not a recipe: spec and tests first worked for me, but people
should find where human checks pay off in their own project.
:::
